- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

3	# Language rules — what catches a break of each one
4	
5	This page is for whoever maintains the catchers. Its companion `docs/language-rules.md` states the rules themselves, in the words a writer applies; this page adds, per rule, its status, what catches a break of it and how far each catcher reads, where each catcher is armed, the rule text the judging model reads, the files that stated the rule in prose before `guardrails/language-rules.json` became its one home, and the notes with their history.
6	
7	It opens with three things a reader needs before any single rule: the status words and the arming events defined, the files that carry the rules, and how to run each kind of catcher over a text by hand. `docs/language-defects.md` is the record of where these rules came from, and it sends a reader here for all of it.
8	
9	The entries stand in the same order as on the writer's page, under the same headings, so one rule is read on both pages by its id.
10	
11	This page is generated from `guardrails/language-rules.json`. A change made here is overwritten by the next run of `scripts/gen-language-consumers.py`, and the gate `guardrails/check-language-rules.py` reds a page that has drifted from the source.
12	
13	## The words on this page
14	
15	The words these rules are stated in. Every page built from this home carries this block, so a reader holding one page holds every word that page uses. A word is defined here when two or more pages need it; a word one page alone needs is defined on that page.
16	
17	- **class** — the shape of a mistake: the form it takes wherever it turns up.
18	- **break** — one place a text falls short of a rule, being a single instance of the class that rule names.
19	- **catcher** — whatever finds a break: a literal pattern in a script, a model reading for meaning, or a person reading the text.
20	- **home** — the one file a given fact is written in.
21	- **the rule home** — the file `guardrails/language-rules.json`, where every rule is edited and nowhere else, and from which every page here is built.
22	- **rule** — one statement about one class, written as one entry in the rule home.
23	- **surface** — a kind of text rather than a file, so one file carries several; this project names six, and each rule binds the ones it applies to.
24	- **stop** — one place a reader could not go on, had to read twice, or had to guess.
25	- **a blocking stop** — a stop where the reader could not go on with the text, or would have acted on the text wrongly; every other stop is one the reader noticed and read past.
26	- **register** — the rules a surface's text is held to: which words, which sentence shapes, and how it addresses its reader.
27	
28	Five roles appear wherever these rules are discussed.
29	
30	- **the writer** — whoever drafts a text: a person, or the agent working for one.
31	- **the reader** — whoever reads that text afterwards, carrying whatever context they happen to have.
32	- **a cold reader** — a reader given the text alone, with no repository, no earlier drafts, and no way to ask the writer a question.
33	- **the maintainer** — whoever builds the catchers and repairs them.
34	- **the owner** — the one person whose project this is.
35	
36	One person often holds more than one of these roles in a day.
37	
38	## The words these pages use
39	
40	A rule's **status** says whether anything catches a break of it today.
41	
42	- `held` — a catcher runs this rule today: at a named harness event, inside a gate, or at a named manual step.
43	- `stated-only` — no catcher runs this rule, which includes a script that exists and is armed nowhere.
44	- `claimed-but-absent` — some file names a catcher for this rule, and that catcher does not carry it.
45	
46	Each **catcher** under a rule carries a status of its own.
47	
48	- `held` — this catcher runs the class it names over the surface it names.
49	- `partial` — this catcher reads part of the class, or part of the surface.
50	- `absent` — no catcher of this kind runs the rule.
51	
52	**Armed at** names the moment a catcher runs, and what a break costs there.
53	
54	- `pre-commit` — a gate refuses the commit until the text changes.
55	- `pre-push` — a gate refuses the push until the text changes.
56	- `session-stop-hook` — the session's reply is held at the end of the turn, and a correction is asked for before the text reaches the reader.
57	- `session-prompt-hook` — the verdict on the previous reply is put in front of the session when the person sends their next message.
58	- `PreToolUse` — the next tool call is denied, so the correction reaches the reader inside the same turn; a rule armed here records it in its notes, since the `armed` field's vocabulary holds no word for the event.
59	- `manual` — a person runs the catcher over a file by hand, and nothing runs it on its own.
60	- `nowhere` — no catcher runs the rule at any event.
61	
62	A rule's **owner** names the one thing that decides a break of it. The status words above say what runs today; the owner says what is meant to run.
63	
64	- `script` — a literal check decides a break of this rule on its own.
65	- `skill` — deciding a break needs a model reading the text for meaning.
66	
67	A path written as `~/...` names the reader's own `.claude` tree, which the package ships to nobody; every other path is relative to the repository root.
68	
69	## The files that carry the rules
70	
71	Every command on this page runs from the repository root, the directory that holds `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`,
72	`guardrails/`, and `scripts/`.
73	
74	- `guardrails/language-rules.json` — the source. Every rule is edited here and nowhere else.
75	- `docs/language-rules.md` — the writer's page, built from the source. A hand edit here is thrown away by the next run
76	  of the generator.
77	- `docs/language-rule-coverage.md` — this page, built from the source and thrown away the same way.
78	- `hooks/language-laws.json` — the rules in the form the judging model reads, built from the source, one body per
79	  catcher and surface.
80	- `scripts/gen-language-consumers.py` — the generator. It reads the source and writes the three built
81	  files above.
82	- `guardrails/check-language-rules.py` — the gate. It refuses a built file that has drifted from the
83	  source, and a rule pointing at a file or a line that is gone.
84	
85	Rebuild the three built files, then check them:
86	
87	```
88	python3 scripts/gen-language-consumers.py
89	python3 guardrails/check-language-rules.py
90	```
91	
92	## Running a catcher by hand
93	
94	Each rule below names its catchers. A rule's **Status** line names the events its catchers are armed
95	at, and the legend above says what a break costs at each of those events.
96	
97	### A script catcher
98	
99	A rule's `pattern` catcher names the file that carries it. Those files are Python scripts, and each
100	takes the text to read as its argument:
101	
102	```
103	python3 guardrails/check-vocabulary.py PRODUCT_SPEC.md
104	python3 scripts/preshow-register-lint.py docs/language-rules.md
105	```
106	
107	Each prints one line on a clean run. A script under `guardrails/` also states how far it read, so its
108	passing verdict says how much of the text it covered.
109	
110	`scripts/preshow-register-lint.py` is one script making two passes over a document that is about to be
111	shown to a person. It always reads the text line by line against its own list of coined phrases, loan
112	translations, and respellings. It also makes the model call described below, and it makes that call
113	only when the environment variable `PRESHOW_REGISTER_JUDGE` is set to `1`, since the call costs a live
114	model run.
115	
116	### The model catcher
117	
118	The model catcher is one model call, made by `hooks/register_judge_core.py`. That module is handed the
119	text together with the rules binding the text's surface, which it reads from `hooks/language-laws.json`, and it
120	answers with the sentences that break one. Two scripts make the call, one on each surface it runs on
121	today.
122	
123	On chat, `hooks/register-judge.py` makes the call. `hooks/register-judge-collect.sh` runs at the
124	session's Stop event, starts that script in the background and returns at once;
125	`hooks/register-judge-report.sh` runs when the person sends their next message and prints whatever
126	verdict landed in the meantime. The person has already read the reply that broke the rule by then, so
127	the correction reaches them one turn later.
128	
129	Making that call by hand needs a session transcript, which the script takes as a Stop-hook payload on
130	its standard input. A transcript is a `.jsonl` file at
131	`~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>.jsonl`, where `<project>` is the working directory's path with
132	its slashes turned into dashes and `<session>` is the session's own identifier. Neither is worth typing
133	out; take the newest transcript on the machine instead:
134	
135	```
136	transcript=$(ls -t ~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl | head -1)
137	printf '{"transcript_path": "%s"}' "$transcript" | python3 hooks/register-judge.py
138	```
139	
140	When the turn breaks a rule, the script prints one JSON line. It names what broke and tells the session
141	to hold its reply until a correction goes out. A clean turn gets no output.
142	
143	On a document, `scripts/preshow-register-lint.py` makes the call, at the moment the document is about
144	to be shown to a person. One call took about 33 seconds when it was measured on 2026-07-17, almost all
145	of it spent starting the `claude` command-line program the call runs through:
146	
147	```
148	PRESHOW_REGISTER_JUDGE=1 python3 scripts/preshow-register-lint.py docs/language-defects.md
149	```
150	
151	Either script stands down on its own breakage: no `claude` binary on the path, a timeout, or an answer
152	the script cannot parse leaves the text unjudged, says so on standard error, and blocks nothing.
153	
154	### A person reading the text
155	
156	A person is the catcher no script and no model replaces, and a reading runs the same way every time.
157	Hand the reader the text alone — no repository, no earlier draft, and no chance to ask the writer a
158	question — together with the job the text is meant to serve, where it serves one. Ask for every place
159	the reading stopped: what the reader stopped on, the guess the reader made there, and whether the stop
160	kept the reader from going on. Write the answer to a dated file under `docs/language-reads/`, and
161	repair the text from those stops rather than from the one sentence in front of you.
162	`docs/language-defects.md` records what every past reading returned and what each one changed.
163	
164	## The rules

Rule text the judging model reads: no coined or jargon term shown to the reader without a plain gloss. 5	This page states every rule this project holds its own texts to, in the words a writer applies to a sentence. Its companion `docs/language-rule-coverage.md` carries the machinery: what catches a break of each rule, how far that catcher reaches, where it is armed, and where the rule was stated before `guardrails/language-rules.json` became its one home. 14	
15	- **class** — the shape of a mistake: the form it takes wherever it turns up.
16	- **break** — one place a text falls short of a rule, being a single instance of the class that rule names.

26	Five roles appear wherever these rules are discussed.

29	- **the reader** — whoever reads that text afterwards, carrying whatever context they happen to have.
30	- **a cold reader** — a reader given the text alone, with no repository, no earlier drafts, and no way to ask the writer a question.
31	- **the maintainer** — whoever builds the catchers and repairs them.
32	- **the owner** — the one person whose project this is.

76	## The words these pages use
77	
78	A rule's **status** says whether anything catches a break of it today.
79	
80	- `held` — a catcher runs this rule today: at a named harness event, inside a gate, or at a named manual step.
81	- `stated-only` — no catcher runs this rule, which includes a script that exists and is armed nowhere.
82	- `claimed-but-absent` — some file names a catcher for this rule, and that catcher does not carry it.
83	
84	Each **catcher** under a rule carries a status of its own.
85	
86	- `held` — this catcher runs the class it names over the surface it names.
87	- `partial` — this catcher reads part of the class, or part of the surface.
88	- `absent` — no catcher of this kind runs the rule.
89	
90	**Armed at** names the moment a catcher runs, and what a break costs there.
91	
92	- `pre-commit` — a gate refuses the commit until the text changes.
93	- `pre-push` — a gate refuses the push until the text changes.
94	- `session-stop-hook` — the session's reply is held at the end of the turn, and a correction is asked for before the text reaches the reader.
95	- `session-prompt-hook` — the verdict on the previous reply is put in front of the session when the person sends their next message.
96	- `PreToolUse` — the next tool call is denied, so the correction reaches the reader inside the same turn; a rule armed here records it in its notes, since the `armed` field's vocabulary holds no word for the event.
97	- `manual` — a person runs the catcher over a file by hand, and nothing runs it on its own.
98	- `nowhere` — no catcher runs the rule at any event.
99	
100	A rule's **owner** names the one thing that decides a break of it. The status words above say what runs today; the owner says what is meant to run.
101	
102	- `script` — a literal check decides a break of this rule on its own.
103	- `skill` — deciding a break needs a model reading the text for meaning.
104	
105	No rule on this page carries a status, and that is deliberate: a rule binds a text whether or not a machine checks it. The words above are defined here because `docs/language-rule-coverage.md` states them of every rule.

940	- `together with the settings ladder` → `together with the four scopes that settle a setting: the session's live word, the host profile, the personal profile, and the package default`

942	### r68 — a placeholder word standing where the thing's own name fits
943	
944	**Rule.** A sentence carries the name of the thing it is about. A pronoun or a general word stands only where the name would clutter the sentence. A status word stands only where the sentence has already stated the condition behind it.

956	### r69 — a step naming a check, a file, or an act with no way to run it or find it
957	
958	**Rule.** A step the reader has to carry out names the command that runs it, or the path that holds it. Where the text can name neither, it says so and names what the reader does instead.
959	
960	**Reader test.** Could a reader carry out this step from the page alone, with nothing else on hand?

968	
969	### r70 — a set claimed whole while the text carries members outside it, or leaves members out with no reason
970	
971	**Rule.** A claim that a set is complete states what the set covers and what it leaves out. The list printed under such a claim carries every member the claim names.
972	
973	**Reader test.** Does the text's own list agree with the claim made over it?
974	
975	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · artifact
976	
977	**Examples.**
978	
979	- `These are every rule binding human-prose.` → `the rules binding human prose, with the printed count and the reason a code is missing`
980	
981	### r71 — a claim resting on ground the reader of the page cannot reach
982	
983	**Rule.** A claim carries its ground on the page that makes it. A file named beside the claim holds the record, and the page still states what the reader needs.
984	
985	**Reader test.** Can a reader holding this page alone see what this claim rests on?
986	
987	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · chat · artifact
988	
989	**Examples.**
990	
991	- `The loop came from the spec-format comprehension gate.` → `what that gate observed, stated on the page, with the file that records it named beside it`
992	- `that run is clean` → `the command that runs the check, and what a passing run prints`
993	
994	### r72 — a number stated without the four parts a measurement carries
995	
996	**Rule.** A number stated to a reader carries four things. They are why it is measured, what changes when it moves, its unit, and the method behind it. The four stand in the number's own sentence or in the paragraph around it. A number quoted from a named source inherits that source's method.
997	
998	**Reader test.** Reading this number alone, do I know what is counted, which decision it informs, and which command gives it again?
999	
1000	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · chat · artifact
1001	
1002	**Examples.**
1003	
1004	- `A reading returned fifteen stops.` → `name the unit, the decision the count informs, what changes when it moves, and the command behind it`
1005	
1006	### r73 — a sentence carrying a second rule or a definition
1007	
1008	**Rule.** One sentence states one rule and holds no definition.
1009	
1010	**Reader test.** Does this sentence state one rule a reader could cite on its own, with no definition folded into it?
1011	
1012	**Binds.** spec-body · human-prose · artifact
1013	
1014	**Examples.**
1015	
1016	- `the orchestration law that the session keeps pulling unblocked queue work while any remains.` → `state the law in one short sentence, and put its parts in a list`
1017	
1018	**Exceptions.** a rhetorical triad, which carries no list.
1019	
1020	### r74 — a domain noun the body uses with no glossary entry
1021	
1022	**Rule.** Every domain noun the body uses holds one glossary entry of one sentence.
1023	
1024	**Reader test.** Does the glossary hold an entry for this noun, and does that entry come before the noun's first working use?
1025	
1026	**Binds.** spec-body
1027	
1028	**Exceptions.** a word of ordinary English, which needs no entry.
1029	
1030	### r75 — a normative sentence binding a vague actor
1031	
1032	**Rule.** A normative sentence names the actor it binds, and that name is the actor that acts.
1033	
1034	**Reader test.** Does this requirement name the actor it binds, and is that the actor that acts?
1035	
1036	**Binds.** spec-body
1037	
1038	**Examples.**
1039	
1040	- `the system` → `the actor that acts, where the document names a finer one`
1041	
1042	**Exceptions.** a region marked informative.
1043	
1044	## An index of questions
1045	
1046	A writer arrives with a question and not yet the name of a defect, and every rule title on this page is written as the name of a defect. Each question below names every rule that answers it.

| факт | A строки | B строки | вердикт | примечание |
|------|----------|----------|---------|-----------|
| Генератор и инфраструктура (header, paths, check-language-rules.py) | 1, 11, 69-90 | 1, 9 | ГЕНЕРЁННОЕ | Оба файла порождены scripts/gen-language-consumers.py; заголовок идентичен |
| Глоссарий "The words on this page" (class, break, catcher, home, rule, surface, stop, register) | 15–26 | 13–24 | ГЕНЕРЁННОЕ | Идентичный список определений в обоих файлах; необходим каждому читателю |
| Роли (the writer, the reader, a cold reader, the maintainer, the owner) | 28–34 | 26–34 | ГЕНЕРЁННОЕ | Совпадает слово в слово; общая часть template'а генератора |
| Статус-лексика (held, stated-only, claimed-but-absent) | 40–44 | 80–82 | ГЕНЕРЁННОЕ | Похожие определения; B добавляет строку 105 уточняя, что эти слова не рангируют правила на B |
| Статус каждого catche'ра (held, partial, absent) | 46–50 | 84–88 | ГЕНЕРЁННОЕ | Идентичные определения |
| Armed at / вооружение события (pre-commit, pre-push, session-stop-hook и т. д.) | 52–60 | 90–98 | ГЕНЕРЁННОЕ | Совпадает полностью |
| Определение Owner (script vs skill) | 62–65 | 100–103 | ГЕНЕРЁННОЕ | Совпадает |
| Заголовок "## The rules" + intro к r01–r75 | 164–178, 184–198 и далее | 107–152 и далее | ДВА-ДОМА | A фокусируется на реализации (что ловит, reach, armed); B на применении (Rule, Reader test, Examples). Разные цели — один факт в двух домах |

**Оценка:**
- **ГЕНЕРЁННОЕ**: ~600–700 байт (header, глоссарий 9 пунктов × 50 байт, роли, статус-лексика)  
  Всё это генерируется один раз в guardrails/language-rules.json и копируется обоим файлам скриптом. Удалить нельзя — читатель каждого файла должен понимать термины без перепрыгивания.

- **ДВА-ДОМА**: Содержимое каждого правила (r01–r75) — одно правило, изложено дважды разными словами под разными углом. Источник общий (guardrails/language-rules.json), но оба изложения необходимы: A для тех, кто строит ловушки ошибок, B для пишущих. Указатели между ними есть (в intro обоих файлов).

- **ШУМ** (структура, 1 строка): section headers, markdown scaffolding — ~50 упоминаний в шинглах, но это просто побочный эффект идентичного layout'а.

Зв. перезаписываемого текста: ~700 байт (терминология) можно было бы заменить ссылкой на одну copy, но это сделало бы оба файла хрупче. Сейчас каждый самостоялен.
